title: Apollo unmasks himself: mortal against immortal
greek: αὐτὸς θνητὸς ἐὼν θεὸν ἄμβροτον (autos thnētos eōn theon ambroton)
short: Apollo, disguised as Agenor, reveals that Achilles has been chasing a god; Achilles answers that he would take revenge on the god if he could.
body: Book 22 opens where Book 21 left off: Apollo, still in Agenor's shape (as Walter Leaf notes), turns and mocks Achilles, 'thyself a mortal', for pursuing an immortal who 'is not appointed to die'. Achilles' reply is startling: 'Verily I would avenge me on thee, had I but the power.' Compare Diomedes in Book 5, who stops when Apollo warns him that gods and men are not alike (5.440-4); Achilles does not retreat in awe but resents the limit. The god he resents is the one who will finally kill him (21.277-8, 22.359-60). The episode also has a practical function: Apollo's trick has bought the Trojans time to get inside the walls, leaving Hector alone outside the Scaean gates.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 22.7-20
Homer, Iliad 5.440-444

title: Achilles as Sirius, the Dog Star
greek: ὅν τε κύν' Ὠρίωνος ἐπίκλησιν καλέουσι (hon te kun' Ōriōnos epiklēsin kaleousi)
short: Priam sees Achilles gleam like Sirius, the brightest star, which rises at harvest time and brings fever: beautiful and deadly at once.
body: Sirius, called 'the Dog of Orion' because it follows the hunter constellation, rises at dawn in high summer, the season (opōrē, 'harvest-time') of heat and fevers; Hesiod links its rising with parching heat (Works and Days 582-8). Homer joins splendour and menace: 'brightest of all is he, yet withal is he a sign of evil'. Walter Leaf points out an astronomical difficulty, since Sirius shines high 'in the darkness of night' only in winter and spring, not at its summer rising, and suggests that the phrase nuktos amolgos may mean twilight rather than deep night. Diomedes was likened to the same 'autumn star' (5.5-6), and Hector to a baleful star (11.62). Virgil imitated the simile for Aeneas (Aeneid 10.272-5). The image is answered at the end of the duel, when Achilles' spear gleams like the evening star (22.317-20), framing the book with two stars, one of fever, one of beauty.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 22.26-31
Hesiod, Works and Days 582-588
Virgil, Aeneid 10.272-275

title: Priam's missing sons and the dramatic irony of his plea
greek: Λυκάονα καὶ Πολύδωρον, τούς μοι Λαοθόη τέκετο (Lukaona kai Poludōron, tous moi Laothoē teketo)
short: Priam hopes his sons Lycaon and Polydorus are prisoners who can be ransomed; the audience knows Achilles has already killed them both.
body: The audience has watched Achilles kill Polydorus (20.407-18) and Lycaon (21.34-135), so Priam's hope of ransoming them 'with bronze and gold' is painful dramatic irony. It also recalls the older world of ransom that Achilles has abandoned (21.99-102). Their mother Laothoe was, Walter Leaf notes, a full wife of Priam, not a concubine: 'genuine polygamy' appears in Homer only among the Trojans, one of the few hints of different customs between the two peoples. Priam tells Achilles in Book 24 that he had fifty sons, nineteen by Hecuba (24.495-7). Leaf doubted the line about the dowry given by Altes (22.51), since gifts to a bride from her father belong, he thought, to the end of the Homeric period, and he suspected the whole passage 46-55 because it weighs the parents' and the people's grief too coolly. Others find the contrast between private and public sorrow effective.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 22.46-53; and Introduction to Book XXII, p. 428
Homer, Iliad 24.495-497

anchor: A young man it beseemeth wholly
title: Priam's plea: the death of the young and the old
greek: νέῳ δέ τε πάντ' ἐπέοικεν ἀρηϊκταμένῳ (neōi de te pant' epeoiken arēiktamenōi)
short: Priam foresees Troy's sack and his corpse mangled by his own dogs, contrasting a young man's fitting death with an old man's shameful one.
body: Priam's speech is a vision of the fall of Troy: sons killed, daughters dragged away, infants dashed to the ground, and himself, the last, killed at his door and eaten by the very dogs he fed at his table. The epic Sack of Ilium told how Priam was killed at the altar of Zeus in his courtyard. Then comes the famous contrast: for a young man killed in war, everything is fitting, 'all is honourable whatsoever be seen'; but dogs defiling the grey head and the nakedness of an old man is 'the most piteous thing'. The Spartan poet Tyrtaeus uses closely similar lines to urge young men not to let older warriors die in front of them (fr. 10.21-30 West). Walter Leaf, who doubted lines 69-76 because the horror is exaggerated, thought it more probable that the interpolator of 69-76 copied Tyrtaeus than the reverse, against the older view that Tyrtaeus was the imitator. The 'threshold of old age' means, Leaf argues, old age itself, not its beginning.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 22.60 and 22.69-76
Tyrtaeus, fragment 10.21-30 West

title: Hecuba bares her breast
greek: κόλπον ἀνιεμένη, ἑτέρηφι δὲ μαζὸν ἀνέσχε (kolpon aniemenē, heterēphi de mazon anesche)
short: Hecuba loosens her robe and holds out the breast that nursed Hector: a mother's supplication, calling on the bond of nurture.
body: Hecuba's gesture is a form of supplication: she appeals not to Zeus or to guest-friendship but to the body that fed her son, 'have thou respect unto this and pity me'. The same verbs, aideomai and eleeō, that Lycaon used to Achilles (21.74) are here a mother's plea to her child. Greek tragedy remembered the gesture: Clytemnestra bares her breast to Orestes as he is about to kill her (Aeschylus, Libation Bearers 896-8). Hecuba calls Hector 'dear plant' (philon thalos), a word for a young shoot, as Thetis speaks of rearing Achilles 'like a sapling' (18.56-7); Walter Leaf notes the masculine agreement that follows the sense rather than the grammar. Her fear is concrete: if Achilles kills him, she cannot lay him on a bier and lament, but dogs will eat him far away by the Argive ships. Neither parent persuades him, and the poet repeats the fact twice (22.78, 91).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 22.80-87

title: Hector as a mountain snake
greek: ὡς δὲ δράκων ἐπὶ χειῇ ὀρέστερος ἄνδρα μένῃσι, βεβρωκὼς κακὰ φάρμακ' (hōs de drakōn epi kheiēi oresteros andra menēisi, bebrōkōs kaka pharmak')
short: Hector waits for Achilles like a snake coiled at its hole, swollen with poison from 'evil herbs': rage, not calm courage.
body: The serpent 'having fed upon evil herbs' reflects a popular belief, reported by Walter Leaf, that snakes made their venom from poisonous plants; Aelian repeats it (On Animals 6.4), and Virgil imitates the passage when Pyrrhus gleams at Priam's door 'like a snake fed on evil herbs' (coluber mala gramina pastus, Aeneid 2.471). The simile shows Hector at a moment of fierce resolve: he leans his shield against a jutting bastion and glares, 'his courage unquenchable'. But a snake at its hole is also a creature at bay, defending its lair, which suits the defender of the city. Leaf adds that the coiling inside the hole reflects human nervousness more than accurate natural history. The resolve will not last: within a few lines Hector is weighing surrender, and when Achilles appears he runs.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 22.93-95
Virgil, Aeneid 2.471-475

anchor: I have shame of the Trojans
title: Hector's shame (aidōs) and his mistake
greek: αἰδέομαι Τρῶας καὶ Τρῳάδας ἑλκεσιπέπλους (aideomai Trōas kai Trōiadas helkesipeplous)
short: Hector cannot go inside: he refused Polydamas' advice to retreat, lost many men, and is ashamed to face the Trojans and their wives.
body: In Book 18 Polydamas urged the Trojans to withdraw into the city once Achilles returned to battle (18.254-83); Hector rejected him scornfully (18.285-309). Now he admits that he has destroyed his people 'through his own recklessness' (atasthaliēisin emēisin), the word the Odyssey's proem uses for the fatal folly of Odysseus' crew. His line 'I feel shame before the Trojans and the Trojan women with trailing robes' repeats exactly what he said to Andromache in Book 6 (6.442), when he explained why he could not stay out of the fighting. Aidōs is the sense of how one appears to one's community; for Hector it now makes retreat impossible. James Redfield's study of the Iliad as 'the tragedy of Hector' takes this monologue as central: Hector's virtues, his responsibility to his people, become the trap that kills him. Gregory Nagy adds that Hector here turns to the hope of dying 'gloriously' (eukleiōs, 22.110).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 22.100-105
James M. Redfield, Nature and Culture in the Iliad: The Tragedy of Hector, Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1975
Gregory Nagy, 'A sampling of comments on Iliad Rhapsody 22', Classical Inquiries (Center for Hellenic Studies, Harvard), 2016, rev. 2018, comment on I.22.110

title: 'But why does my heart debate this?': the monologue of decision
greek: ἀλλὰ τί ἤ μοι ταῦτα φίλος διελέξατο θυμός; (alla ti ē moi tauta philos dielexato thumos?)
short: A formula that closes a hero's inner debate and turns him to fight; it appears in five Iliadic monologues, and Hector's is the climax.
body: Homeric heroes sometimes speak 'to their own great-hearted spirit' (thumos) at a crisis. Four such monologues follow one pattern: the hero considers flight, sees its shame, and breaks off with this line before resolving to stand: Odysseus (11.407), Menelaus (17.97), Agenor (21.562) and Hector here. Bernard Fenik's study of these 'four monologues' shows how a fixed pattern allows variation, and Walter Leaf sets out the shared scheme of Agenor's and Hector's speeches. Hector's alternative is the most extraordinary: he imagines laying down his arms and offering Achilles Helen, her treasure and half of Troy's wealth, before rejecting the fantasy. The line recurs later in this book in Achilles' mouth (22.385), where Leaf thought it out of place, since it normally ends a debate with oneself. Murray's 'hold converse with me' translates dielexato, 'talked through, debated'.

sources.cite: Bernard Fenik, 'Stylization and variety: four monologues in the Iliad', in B. Fenik (ed.), Homer: Tradition and Invention, Leiden: Brill, 1978
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 22.98 and 22.385; cf. note on 21.552
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed., s.v. διαλέγομαι

title: 'From oak or from rock': a proverb
greek: οὐ μέν πως νῦν ἔστιν ἀπὸ δρυὸς οὐδ' ἀπὸ πέτρης τῷ ὀαριζέμεναι (ou men pōs nun estin apo druos oud' apo petrēs tōi oarizemenai)
short: Hector says this is no time to chat with Achilles 'from oak or rock' like a youth and a maiden: an old proverb whose exact sense is debated.
body: The phrase 'from oak or from rock' is clearly proverbial, but its meaning is uncertain. Penelope uses it to Odysseus: 'you were not born from an oak of old story, or from a rock' (Od. 19.163), and Hesiod breaks off with 'but what is this to me, about oak or rock?' (Theogony 35). Walter Leaf thinks the words carried an allusion now lost, perhaps to an old tale of men born from trees and stones, and that here they mean idle talk, the kind of tale a lover tells; he rejects the idea of a rustic lovers' seat. A. B. Cook argued that oarizein, 'to chat intimately', could also mean a warrior's boastful challenge, but Leaf found this too harsh. Gregory Nagy discusses the proverb as a marker of myth-telling. The repetition 'youth and maiden, youth and maiden' was admired by ancient critics and condemned by some moderns. Its effect is bitter: the language of courtship surfaces just as Hector rejects any parley with a man who will not pity him.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 22.126-128
Gregory Nagy, 'A sampling of comments on Iliad Rhapsody 22', Classical Inquiries (Center for Hellenic Studies, Harvard), 2016, rev. 2018, comment on I.22.122-130
Hesiod, Theogony 35
Homer, Odyssey 19.163

anchor: As a falcon in the mountains
title: Achilles as falcon, Hector as dove
greek: ἠΰτε κίρκος ὄρεσφιν, ἐλαφρότατος πετεηνῶν, ῥηϊδίως οἴμησε μετὰ τρήρωνα πέλειαν (ēute kirkos oresphin, elaphrotatos peteēnōn, rhēidiōs oimēse meta trērōna peleian)
short: Hector flees and Achilles swoops after him like a falcon after a trembling dove: the image used playfully of Artemis now returns in earnest.
body: Hector's nerve breaks at the sight of Achilles, 'peer of Enyalius', with the bronze flashing like fire or the rising sun, and the chase begins. The kirkos is a hawk or falcon, 'swiftest of winged things'. In Book 21 the same pair of birds described Artemis fleeing Hera, with the reassurance that it was 'not her lot to be taken' (21.493-6); here there is no such escape. The simile also stresses speed, the defining quality of 'swift-footed Achilles', and fear, since Hector, the bravest Trojan, now runs. The poem's treatment of his flight is not contemptuous: the narrator later insists that 'in front a good man fled, but one mightier far pursued' (22.158). Several further similes (the hound and fawn, 22.189-93; the dream, 22.199-201) vary the image of a pursuit that cannot end until the gods decide it.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 22.139
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed., s.v. κίρκος

title: The two springs of the Scamander and the washing-tanks
greek: κρουνὼ δ' ἵκανον καλλιρρόω, ἔνθα δὲ πηγαὶ δοιαὶ ἀναΐσσουσι Σκαμάνδρου δινήεντος (krounō d' hikanon kallirroō, entha de pēgai doiai anaïssousi Skamandrou dinēentos)
short: The chase passes a hot and a cold spring and the stone tanks where Trojan women washed clothes in peacetime; travellers have long searched for the site.
body: One spring steams 'as from a blazing fire', the other runs cold as ice even in summer. Strabo already noticed that no hot spring could be found near Troy and that the Scamander rises in the mountains, not at the city (13.1.43). The French traveller Lechevalier thought he had found the two springs at Pınarbaşı (Bounarbashi), which for decades made that hill the favourite site for Troy; later investigators found many springs there, all of about the same temperature. Walter Leaf notes that the true sources of the Menderes on Mount Ida are two great springs of different temperature, about twenty miles away, and concludes that the poet built his landscape from reports rather than personal knowledge. The detail of the washing-troughs, where wives and daughters washed 'in the time of peace, before the sons of the Achaeans came', is one of Homer's most poignant glimpses of ordinary life, placed at the moment of greatest danger. Jasper Griffin discusses such contrasts between peace and war.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 22.145-156
Strabo, Geography 13.1.43
Jasper Griffin, Homer on Life and Death, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1980

title: A race for Hector's life
greek: οὐχ ἱερήϊον οὐδὲ βοείην ἀρνύσθην, ἅ τε ποσσὶν ἀέθλια γίγνεται ἀνδρῶν, ἀλλὰ περὶ ψυχῆς θέον Ἕκτορος ἱπποδάμοιο (oukh hierēion oude boeiēn arnusthēn ... alla peri psukhēs theon Hektoros hippodamoio)
short: The chase is pictured as an athletic contest whose prize is not an ox or a hide but Hector's life, anticipating the funeral games of Book 23.
body: The narrator turns the pursuit into a sporting event: men race for a sacrificial animal or an oxhide, chariots wheel round the turning-post for 'a tripod haply or a woman, in honour of a warrior that is dead'. These are the prizes of funeral games, and Book 23 will show exactly such games for Patroclus. Walter Leaf notes that Heyne suspected 162-5 as later, but that line 165, 'these twain circled thrice', is indispensable. Aristotle cites the pursuit as something that would be absurd on stage (the other Greeks standing still) but works in epic narration (Poetics 24, 1460a). Some ancient critics, thinking three circuits impossible, tried to take 'around the city' as 'near the city'; Leaf answers that a triple circuit of Hissarlik is hard but possible. Virgil kept the number: Hector was 'thrice dragged around the walls of Troy' (Aeneid 1.483). An earlier simile already compared Achilles to a prize-winning racehorse (22.22-4). The sporting language makes the horror sharper: the prize is a life.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 22.159-165
Aristotle, Poetics 24, 1460a11-17
Virgil, Aeneid 1.483

anchor: all the gods gazed upon them
title: The gods as spectators: Zeus thinks of saving Hector
greek: θεοὶ δ' ἐς πάντες ὁρῶντο (theoi d' es pantes horōnto)
short: The gods watch the chase like an audience; Zeus pities Hector, a pious sacrificer, and proposes to save him, but Athena objects and Zeus yields.
body: Zeus grieves for Hector, who 'hath burned for me many thighs of oxen' on Ida and in the citadel, and asks the gods whether to save him. Athena answers, 'A man that is mortal, doomed long since by fate, art thou minded to deliver again?' Her words repeat almost exactly Hera's reply when Zeus wished to save his own son Sarpedon (16.440-3 = 22.179-81). Jasper Griffin has shown how the gods' role as spectators shapes the Iliad: their gaze lends the human contest importance, while their freedom from death makes their pity and their withdrawal all the more striking. Walter Leaf, on the other hand, argued that the scene interrupts the race at its highest tension and anticipates the weighing of fates (22.208-13), and suspected that 166-207 were added. Zeus' reply, 'I do not speak with full purpose of heart', shows the limits of even the highest god's will before fate.

sources.cite: Jasper Griffin, Homer on Life and Death, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1980
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 22.166-185; and Introduction to Book XXII, p. 428
Homer, Iliad 16.431-461

title: The dream simile
greek: ὡς δ' ἐν ὀνείρῳ οὐ δύναται φεύγοντα διώκειν (hōs d' en oneirōi ou dunatai pheugonta diōkein)
short: Pursuer and pursued are like figures in a nightmare, one unable to catch, the other unable to escape. Aristarchus rejected the lines; Virgil imitated them.
body: 'As in a dream a man availeth not to pursue one that fleeth before him, the one availeth not to flee, nor the other to pursue.' The simile captures the paralysis of the race: speed has turned into stasis. Aristarchus athetized lines 199-201, judging them cheap in style and thought and inconsistent with the image of speed elsewhere. Walter Leaf answers that one simile may introduce the chase with speed and another close it with exhausted helplessness, and admires the precision: the comparison is not to failing to catch someone in a dream, which would be commonplace, but to the dreamer's feeling of being unable even to move. Virgil confirms the effect by imitating it at the climax of the Aeneid, when Turnus, facing Aeneas, is like a dreamer whose limbs fail him (Aeneid 12.908-12). Leaf nonetheless thought the passage part of a later expansion (22.166-207).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 22.199-201; and Appendix K
Virgil, Aeneid 12.908-912

title: No one else may strike Hector: glory (kudos) for one man
greek: μή τις κῦδος ἄροιτο βαλών, ὁ δὲ δεύτερος ἔλθοι (mē tis kudos aroito balōn, ho de deuteros elthoi)
short: Achilles signals to the Achaeans not to throw at Hector, lest another win the glory and he come second.
body: The Achaean army is present but silent: Achilles forbids them to shoot, 'lest another might smite him and win glory, and himself come too late'. The motive is kudos, the glory of victory, which cannot be shared. Earlier Achilles had warned Patroclus not to take too much glory for himself (16.87-90); now he guards Hector's death as his personal revenge and his personal triumph. Walter Leaf regarded these lines as an explanatory addition meant to answer the obvious question why no other Greek intervenes; he also noted that, apart from Achilles and Patroclus, no Greek hero is named in the whole book, an artistic reticence that isolates the duel. Leaf compares 10.368, where Diomedes chases Dolon 'lest one of the Achaeans should boast that he struck first'. The isolation of the two men becomes complete when the gods weigh their fates.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 22.205-207; and Introduction to Book XXII, pp. 427-8
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed., s.v. κῦδος

title: The golden scales of Zeus (the weighing of fates)
greek: καὶ τότε δὴ χρύσεια πατὴρ ἐτίταινε τάλαντα (kai tote dē khruseia patēr etitaine talanta)
short: On the fourth circuit Zeus weighs two fates of death; Hector's sinks towards Hades, and Apollo abandons him.
body: Zeus places two kēres, 'fates of death', on the scales, one for each man, and lifts them by the middle; 'down sank the day of doom of Hector'. The same image decided a whole day of battle in Book 8 (8.69-74), and the 'sacred scales of Zeus' are mentioned at 16.658 and as a metaphor of the fortunes of war at 19.223-4. Walter Leaf explains the idea as a metaphor become belief: the rise and fall of the scales pictures the changing fortunes of war, and the scales come to stand for the will of fate itself. Plutarch reports that Aeschylus built a whole tragedy, the lost Psychostasia ('Weighing of Souls'), on this scene, transferring it to Achilles and Memnon; the Egyptian weighing of souls may also lie behind later versions. Virgil uses the scales when Aeneas fights Turnus (Aeneid 12.725-7). The moment the scale sinks, 'Phoebus Apollo left him': the god who has sustained Hector withdraws, and Athena arrives.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 22.209-213
Plutarch, How the Young Man Should Study Poetry 17A (on Aeschylus' Psychostasia)
Virgil, Aeneid 12.725-727

title: Athena's deception: the false Deiphobus
greek: Δηϊφόβῳ ἐϊκυῖα δέμας καὶ ἀτειρέα φωνήν (Dēiphobōi eikuia demas kai ateirea phōnēn)
short: Athena takes the form of Hector's favourite brother Deiphobus, persuades him to stand, and then vanishes when he calls for a second spear.
body: Athena's trick is the cruellest divine intervention in the poem. Disguised as Deiphobus, 'far the dearest of my brethren', she pretends to have defied their parents to stand beside Hector; when Hector's spear rebounds and he calls for another, there is no one there. Hector understands at once: 'the gods have called me to my death ... Athene hath beguiled me.' Walter Leaf found the intervention 'at once so revolting and so needless' to a modern reader, but argued that an ancient audience would see divine help as a sign that Achilles had heaven's will on his side. Gregory Nagy sees a long-standing hostility of Athena towards Hector, the protector of the city whose own patron she is, and reads this speech as the end of Hector's delusion. Athena also returns Achilles' thrown spear 'unseen of Hector', a detail that makes the duel unequal and has troubled readers since antiquity.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 22.226-247 and 22.299; and Introduction to Book XXII, p. 429
Gregory Nagy, 'A sampling of comments on Iliad Rhapsody 22', Classical Inquiries (Center for Hellenic Studies, Harvard), 2016, rev. 2018, comment on I.22.297-305

title: Hector's proposed oath: the return of the body
greek: ἀλλ' ἄγε δεῦρο θεοὺς ἐπιδώμεθα· τοὶ γὰρ ἄριστοι μάρτυροι ἔσσονται καὶ ἐπίσκοποι ἁρμονιάων (all' age deuro theous epidōmetha; toi gar aristoi marturoi essontai kai episkopoi harmoniaōn)
short: Hector proposes a sworn agreement that the winner will strip the loser's armour but return his body for burial. Achilles refuses.
body: Oaths in Homer are sworn with the gods as witnesses and guardians; Walter Leaf explains Hector's phrase as each man 'giving' his gods as guarantors of the agreement, as in the formal oath before the duel of Paris and Menelaus (3.276-91). Hector has proposed this before: in Book 7, challenging the best of the Achaeans, he promised to return his victim's body so that he could be buried and have a mound by the Hellespont (7.76-91). The return of the corpse was the minimum decency of heroic warfare, since burial secured a man's rest and his memory. Hector's offer is generous and also self-interested, for he already fears for his own body. Achilles' refusal, couched in the language of beasts, sets up the main moral problem of the last books: who will bury Hector, and on what terms? The answer comes only in Book 24, through Priam's supplication and the gods' command.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 22.254-261
Homer, Iliad 7.76-91
Charles Segal, The Theme of the Mutilation of the Corpse in the Iliad (Mnemosyne Supplement 17), Leiden: Brill, 1971

title: 'No oaths between lions and men'
greek: ὡς οὐκ ἔστι λέουσι καὶ ἀνδράσιν ὅρκια πιστά, οὐδὲ λύκοι τε καὶ ἄρνες ὁμόφρονα θυμὸν ἔχουσιν (hōs ouk esti leousi kai andrasin horkia pista, oude lukoi te kai arnes homophrona thumon ekhousin)
short: Achilles rejects any pact: as lions and men, wolves and lambs, cannot swear oaths, neither can he and Hector. He places himself outside human society.
body: Achilles answers Hector's offer with an 'angry glance from beneath his brows'. He calls Hector alaste, which Murray renders 'madman'; it is more nearly 'accursed, unforgettable (wrong-doer)', a man whose deeds cannot be forgotten. Then comes the comparison: there are no trustworthy oaths between lions and men, and wolves and lambs never share one mind. Oaths belong to the human community; by placing himself and Hector in the relation of predator and prey, Achilles steps outside it. Gregory Nagy notes how this links to the lion imagery attached to Achilles, who is called 'lion-hearted' (7.228) and whose menos and thumos drive him like a lion's (20.164-75); the same forces will produce his wish to eat Hector's flesh raw (22.346-7). The speech ends with the demand that Hector 'pay back the full price' of Achilles' grief for his comrades, the logic of revenge rather than of exchange.

anchor: men that are yet to be
title: Hector's last resolve: glory for future generations
greek: μὴ μὰν ἀσπουδί γε καὶ ἀκλειῶς ἀπολοίμην, ἀλλὰ μέγα ῥέξας τι καὶ ἐσσομένοισι πυθέσθαι (mē man aspoudi ge kai akleiōs apoloimēn, alla mega rhexas ti kai essomenoisi puthesthai)
short: Knowing he is doomed, Hector resolves not to die without a struggle or 'without glory' (akleiōs), but in some great deed for men to hear of later.
body: This is the purest statement of the heroic ideal in the poem, spoken by a man who knows he will lose. Kleos is what is heard (from kluein, 'to hear'): fame carried in song to 'men that are yet to be'. Gregory Nagy points out that Hector's words a-kleiōs 'without glory' answer his earlier hope to die eu-kleiōs 'gloriously' (22.110), and that Andromache's lament ends by acknowledging exactly this ambition (22.514). The irony is that the Iliad itself fulfils the wish: Hector's last stand is what later generations hear. He draws his sword and swoops 'like an eagle of lofty flight' on a lamb or hare, but the simile is bitter, because he is in fact the prey. Compare Achilles' choice between a long life and kleos aphthiton, 'unwithering glory' (9.410-16): both heroes accept death in exchange for fame.

title: Achilles' spear like the Evening Star
greek: οἷος δ' ἀστὴρ εἶσι μετ' ἀστράσι νυκτὸς ἀμολγῷ ἕσπερος, ὃς κάλλιστος ἐν οὐρανῷ ἵσταται ἀστήρ (hoios d' astēr eisi met' astrasi nuktos amolgōi hesperos, hos kallistos en ouranōi histatai astēr)
short: The point of Achilles' spear gleams like Hesperus, 'fairest of all stars', as he looks for the opening in Hector's armour.
body: The book's second star simile completes a frame. Achilles first appeared to Priam like Sirius, brilliant and deadly (22.26-31); now the gleam of his spear-point is like the Evening Star, 'the fairest of all'. Beauty and death coincide: the loveliest light in the sky shines on the weapon at the moment it kills. Walter Leaf notes the same puzzle about 'the darkness of night' as in the Sirius simile and suggests that Venus can shine brilliantly until a fairly late hour in winter. Just before, Achilles' helmet with its golden plumes, made by Hephaestus, has been described (22.314-16), and Leaf thinks the second line of that description is borrowed from Book 19. Hesperus is the star that brings everything home in Sappho (fr. 104 Voigt), a resonance that sharpens the contrast here, as Hector will never come home.

title: The fatal wound and Patroclus' armour
greek: φαίνετο δ' ᾗ κληῗδες ἀπ' ὤμων αὐχέν' ἔχουσι, λαυκανίην (phaineto d' hēi klēides ap' ōmōn aukhen' ekhousi, laukaniēn)
short: Hector wears Achilles' own former armour, stripped from Patroclus; Achilles knows its one gap, at the throat, and strikes there.
body: Hector stripped Achilles' old armour from Patroclus' body and put it on (17.192-7). So Achilles, now in new armour made by Hephaestus, faces his own former equipment and knows exactly where it leaves the body open: where the collar-bones join neck and shoulders, 'even the gullet' (laukaniē). The spear goes through the neck but does not cut the windpipe (asphargos), 'to the end that he might yet make answer'. Aristarchus athetized that line (22.329) as ridiculous, as if the spear took care to leave Hector able to speak; Walter Leaf thought the anatomical explanation looks like a rhapsode's answer to a pedantic question, since 'the poet in this great climax of pathos has higher matters to think of than anatomical realism'. Leaf also noted that Achilles' first taunt is shaped to echo Hector's own boast over Patroclus (16.830-42). The armour makes the killing a mirror: Achilles in a sense kills an image of himself.

title: Achilles' cannibal wish
greek: αἲ γάρ πως αὐτόν με μένος καὶ θυμὸς ἀνήῃ ὤμ' ἀποταμνόμενον κρέα ἔδμεναι (ai gar pōs auton me menos kai thumos anēēi ōm' apotamnomenon krea edmenai)
short: Refusing Hector's plea, Achilles wishes his fury would let him cut up Hector's flesh and eat it raw: rage at the edge of the inhuman.
body: Hector begs 'by thy life and knees and parents' that his body be returned for burning. Achilles replies 'Implore me not, dog', and wishes his menos and thumos would drive him to carve and eat Hector raw. Walter Leaf argues that the wish expresses something inconceivable, not a memory of real cannibalism, and compares the idiom in which a certainty is stressed by contrast with an impossibility. Homer uses the same extreme image twice more: Zeus tells Hera she would like to eat Priam and his sons raw (4.34-6), and Hecuba wishes she could fasten her teeth in Achilles' liver (24.212-13). Gregory Nagy connects the wish to the lion imagery of Achilles a few lines earlier: raw flesh is a predator's food. The passage marks the furthest point of Achilles' dehumanization, from which Book 24 will bring him back.

title: Ransom refused: 'not for your weight in gold'
greek: οὐδ' εἴ κέν σ' αὐτὸν χρυσῷ ἐρύσασθαι ἀνώγοι Δαρδανίδης Πρίαμος (oud' ei ken s' auton khrusōi erusasthai anōgoi Dardanidēs Priamos)
short: Achilles swears he will not give up the body for tenfold or twentyfold ransom, not even for Hector's weight in gold: a vow Book 24 will overturn.
body: Ransom (apoina) of the living and the dead was a normal practice in Homeric war: Priam hoped to buy back Lycaon and Polydorus (22.49-51), and Chryses came to ransom his daughter in Book 1. Achilles rejects it in a rising series of refusals that recalls his answer to Agamemnon's gifts in Book 9 (9.379-87): not ten times, not twenty times, not 'thy weight in gold'. Walter Leaf explains that the Greek means literally 'to weigh thy body against gold', and that the change of mood marks this as an impossible exaggeration. Yet in Book 24 Priam does come with a great ransom, and Achilles accepts it (24.229-37, 24.594-5). Later Greek poets made the hyperbole literal: in Aeschylus' lost play The Phrygians (or The Ransoming of Hector) Hector's body was reportedly weighed against gold. Achilles' vow and its later reversal measure the change in him between Books 22 and 24.

title: 'A heart of iron'
greek: ἦ γὰρ σοί γε σιδήρεος ἐν φρεσὶ θυμός (ē gar soi ge sidēreos en phresi thumos)
short: The dying Hector says Achilles' heart is 'of iron': the metaphor of unyielding hardness that Book 24 will use again, of both Achilles and Priam.
body: Iron in Homer is a rarer, newer metal than bronze, used for tools and as a symbol of hardness; weapons are almost always bronze. 'A heart of iron' (sidēreos thumos) means a heart that cannot be bent by pity. The phrase returns significantly in Book 24: Hecuba calls Priam's heart 'of iron' for daring to go to Achilles (24.205), and Achilles himself says the same of Priam when the old man arrives in his hut (24.521). The repetition transfers the word from cruelty to courage, and from Achilles to the father who melts him. Penelope's heart is called iron by Odysseus for the same unbending quality (Od. 23.172). Walter Leaf links Hector's whole dying speech to Patroclus' death: both dying men see the future clearly, and Hector's insight follows at once in his prophecy.

title: Hector's dying prophecy of Achilles' death
greek: ἤματι τῷ ὅτε κέν σε Πάρις καὶ Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων ἐσθλὸν ἐόντ' ὀλέσωσιν ἐνὶ Σκαιῇσι πύλῃσιν (ēmati tōi hote ken se Paris kai Phoibos Apollōn esthlon eont' olesōsin eni Skaiēisi pulēisin)
short: Hector foretells that Paris and Apollo will kill Achilles at the Scaean gate; Achilles accepts his fate whenever the gods send it.
body: As Patroclus' dying words foretold Hector's death (16.851-4), Hector's foretell Achilles'. Walter Leaf notes that the parallel is deliberate, and that the phrase 'lest I bring the wrath of the gods upon thee' (theōn mēnima) recurs in the Odyssey when the ghost of Elpenor asks for burial (Od. 11.73), so that it reflects a belief that an unburied dead man can bring divine anger on the living. The Iliad never narrates Achilles' death, but it was told in the Aethiopis, which (in Proclus' summary) has him killed by Paris and Apollo at the Scaean gates. Achilles' reply, 'my fate will I accept whenso Zeus willeth', repeats the resolve he made after Patroclus' death (18.115-16). The pairing of the two deaths, Patroclus-Hector and Hector-Achilles, forms a chain of killings that the poem carries beyond its own end.

title: The soul goes to Hades: the formula of heroic death
greek: ψυχὴ δ' ἐκ ῥεθέων πταμένη Ἄϊδόσδε βεβήκει, ὃν πότμον γοόωσα, λιποῦσ' ἀνδροτῆτα καὶ ἥβην (psukhē d' ek rhetheōn ptamenē Aidosde bebēkei, hon potmon goaōsa, lipous' androtēta kai hēbēn)
short: The same two lines describe the deaths of Patroclus and Hector: the psychē flies from the limbs to Hades, mourning its fate, leaving manhood and youth.
body: These lines are used only twice in the Iliad, for Patroclus (16.855-7) and Hector, binding the two deaths together. The psychē in Homer is not the personality but the life-breath that leaves the body and becomes a shadowy image in Hades; the self, in a sense, stays with the corpse, which is why burial matters so much. The word androtēs, 'manhood', has puzzled scholars: Walter Leaf discusses its odd metre and the variant readings, and records Aristarchus' view that it means 'human nature' rather than 'courage', for which Homer says ēnoreē. Leaf suggests a difference like that between 'manhood' and 'manliness'. The soul 'bewailing its fate' expresses the special pathos of a young man's death, the contrast Priam drew earlier in the book (22.71-6). Achilles' reply over the dead body, 'Lie thou dead', is spoken to a corpse that can no longer hear.

anchor: softer is Hector for the handling
title: The Achaeans wound the corpse
greek: ὢ πόποι, ἦ μάλα δὴ μαλακώτερος ἀμφαφάασθαι Ἕκτωρ (ō popoi, ē mala dē malakōteros amphaphaasthai Hektōr)
short: The Achaeans gaze at Hector's beauty, then each stabs the body, joking that he is 'softer to handle' than when he burned the ships.
body: Two reactions follow in quick succession: the soldiers marvel at 'the stature and wondrous comeliness' of the dead man, and then not one of them comes near without wounding him. The jest about Hector being 'softer to handle' now than when he set fire to the ships (Book 16) has the brutal humour of the battlefield. Walter Leaf compares Herodotus' account of the Greeks admiring the body of the Persian Masistius at Plataea (9.25), and a similar taunt in the Icelandic Njal's Saga. He mentions explanations that have been offered for the stabbing: a belief that a mutilated body leaves a harmless ghost, or each man taking revenge for kin killed by Hector. Gregory Nagy treats it as the first stage of the degradation of Hector's body, which the dragging will intensify. In Book 24 Hermes tells Priam that the wounds have all closed up (24.419-21): the gods protect what men try to deface.

title: The paean, song of victory
greek: νῦν δ' ἄγ' ἀείδοντες παιήονα, κοῦροι Ἀχαιῶν (nun d' ag' aeidontes paiēona, kouroi Akhaiōn)
short: Achilles calls on the young Achaeans to sing the paean as they return to the ships; the next two lines may be the words of the song itself.
body: The paean (paiēōn) was a choral song, originally linked with Apollo the healer, sung to give thanks, to avert evil, or to celebrate deliverance. In Book 1 the young Achaeans sing a paean all day to appease Apollo after the plague (1.472-4). Here it is a victory song, a use that became standard in later Greece, where armies sang a paean before and after battle. A marginal note in one medieval manuscript, reported by Walter Leaf, observes that the following lines, 'We have won us great glory; we have slain goodly Hector, to whom the Trojans made prayer throughout their city, as unto a god', are the paean itself, put into the soldiers' mouths; Leaf calls this 'an ingenious observation which has been widely accepted'. Aristarchus athetized the two lines as too boastful. The irony is sharp: Apollo, god of the paean, is the Trojans' protector, and Hecuba will soon say that the Trojans greeted Hector 'as a god' (22.434-5).

title: The dragging of Hector
greek: Ἕκτορα δῖον ἀεικέα μήδετο ἔργα (Hektora dion aeikea mēdeto erga)
short: Achilles pierces Hector's heels, ties the body to his chariot and drags it in the dust towards the ships: 'unseemly deeds', the narrator says.
body: The narrator's own word, aeikea, 'unseemly, shameful', marks the deed as degrading to both victim and doer, as Gregory Nagy emphasises. Achilles cuts through the tendons behind both ankles, threads oxhide straps through them and drags the body behind his chariot, the once-beautiful head trailing in the dust: 'now had Zeus given him over to his foes to suffer foul entreatment in his own native land'. Walter Leaf, quoting a note by A. Macalister on Vesalius, reports that the anatomical 'Achilles tendon' was so named from this passage, not from Achilles' own vulnerable heel. Later tradition reshaped the scene: in Sophocles Hector is dragged by the belt that Ajax had given him (Ajax 1029-31), and Virgil has him 'thrice dragged around the walls of Ilium' (Aeneid 1.483) and shows his swollen, pierced feet (2.272-3). In Homer the dragging around the walls is not narrated; Achilles drags the body to the ships, and later round Patroclus' tomb (24.14-18). Charles Segal shows how this outrage drives the poem towards its resolution, in which the gods preserve the body from harm.

title: Mourning and the laments (gooi) for Hector
greek: Τρῳῇσιν δ' Ἑκάβη ἁδινοῦ ἐξῆρχε γόοιο (Trōiēisin d' Hekabē hadinou exērkhe gooio)
short: Hector's family mourns in the traditional forms: hair torn, veil thrown off, Priam rolling in filth, and formal laments led by the nearest kin.
body: The gestures are those of Greek mourning: Hecuba tears her hair and flings away her veil; Priam grovels 'in the filth' (kopros, the dung of the palace courtyard, as Walter Leaf explains), as he will again in Book 24 (24.163-5). The laments are góoi, personal dirges sung by close relatives, with the community answering in refrain ('thereto the townsfolk added their laments'). Margaret Alexiou's study traces this pattern of leader and responding chorus from Homer to modern Greek folk lament. The book gives three laments, by Priam, Hecuba and Andromache; Book 24 will give three more at Hector's funeral, by Andromache, Hecuba and Helen (24.723-76). Hecuba's words, 'thou that wast my boast night and day ... who ever greeted thee as a god', make Hector the glory of the whole city. Gregory Nagy notes the antiphonal form, the women 'wailing in response' at the end of Andromache's lament (22.515).

anchor: a purple web of double fold
title: Andromache at her loom; the bath that waits for Hector
greek: δίπλακα πορφυρέην, ἐν δὲ θρόνα ποικίλ' ἔπασσε (diplaka porphureēn, en de throna poikil' epasse)
short: Andromache, not yet knowing, weaves flowers into a purple cloth and orders a hot bath for Hector's return; 'unwitting one', comments the poet.
body: Andromache is in the inner part of the house, weaving a double purple cloak and working in 'flowers of varied hue' (throna). Gregory Nagy notes that throna can mean both flower patterns and love charms, and compares Helen weaving the story of the war in Book 3 (3.125-8). Walter Leaf discusses whether floral patterns are plausible in early weaving. She orders her maids to heat a tripod so that Hector may have a hot bath when he returns from battle, 'unwitting one, neither wist she anywise that far from all baths' Athena had laid him low. The narrator's comment (nēpiē, 'poor fool, innocent') is one of the most poignant in Homer. Simone Weil quotes these lines in 'The Iliad, or the Poem of Force' (1940), remarking that most of human life, then as now, goes on far from hot baths. Hearing the cries, Andromache trembles and the shuttle falls from her hand, the domestic work broken by the news.

title: Andromache's headdress and veil (krēdemnon)
greek: ἄμπυκα, κεκρύφαλόν τε ἰδὲ πλεκτὴν ἀναδέσμην κρήδεμνόν θ' (ampuka, kekruphalon te ide plektēn anadesmēn krēdemnon th')
short: Seeing Hector dragged, Andromache faints and her headdress falls: the wedding veil given by Aphrodite, symbol of her marriage and of Troy's 'veil' of walls.
body: Andromache runs to the wall 'like a maenad' (Murray: 'as one beside herself'), sees the body, and falls in a faint described in the language of death: night covers her eyes and she 'gasped forth her spirit'. Her headdress falls: frontlet (ampux), cap or snood (kekruphalos), woven band (anadesmē) and veil (krēdemnon), the last a gift of Aphrodite on the day Hector led her from her father's house 'after he had brought bride-gifts past counting' (hedna). Walter Leaf reports Helbig's and Studniczka's different reconstructions of these items. Gregory Nagy reads the dropped krēdemnon as a ritual miming of Andromache's loss of control over her own fate and of her coming sexual humiliation as a captive, comparing Demeter tearing her veil in the Homeric Hymn (40-2). The word also has a civic meaning: Achilles speaks of loosening Troy's 'sacred krēdemna', its battlements (16.100), a link explored by Michael Nagler. As Andromache's veil falls, so will the city's.

title: The orphan's fate: Andromache's picture of Astyanax
greek: ἦμαρ δ' ὀρφανικὸν παναφήλικα παῖδα τίθησι (ēmar d' orphanikon panaphēlika paida tithēsi)
short: Andromache imagines her son as a fatherless beggar, pushed from other men's feasts; Aristarchus rejected the passage as unsuited to a prince.
body: Andromache paints a scene of social humiliation: the orphan's lands are taken, he goes with head bowed to his father's friends, gets a sip from a cup that wets his lips but not his palate, and is driven from the feast by a boy whose parents are both alive (amphithalēs) with the words 'No father of thine feasteth in our company.' Aristarchus athetized lines 487-99, objecting that such destitution is absurd for a grandson of Priam while his uncles live, and that the passage is a general commonplace about orphanhood; Walter Leaf agreed and thought the athetesis did not go far enough. Leaf adds that the amphithalēs child was thought lucky and favoured by the gods in Greek and Roman ritual. Many readers defend the passage as the voice of a mother's fear rather than a realistic forecast. Andromache then explains her son's name, Astyanax, 'lord of the city', because Hector alone defended Troy; Gregory Nagy notes that Hector's own name means 'holder, protector'. The real fate awaiting the child, being thrown from the walls, was told in the epic Sack of Troy.

title: Burning Hector's clothes: honour without a body
greek: ἀλλ' ἤτοι τάδε πάντα καταφλέξω πυρὶ κηλέῳ (all' ētoi tade panta kataphlexō puri kēleōi)
short: Since Hector's naked body lies by the ships, Andromache will burn the fine clothes woven for him, as an honour to him from the men and women of Troy.
body: Andromache's last words turn to funeral custom. The dead were burned with their clothing and possessions, which accompanied them into the next world. Hector lies naked by the ships, to be eaten by 'writhing worms when the dogs have had their fill'; so she will burn the woven garments in the house, 'in no wise a profit unto thee, seeing thou shalt not lie therein, but to be an honour unto thee from the men and women of Troy'. Walter Leaf explains that without the body the clothes cannot go with Hector, but the burning still serves as a funeral rite that honours him and consoles the living; elsewhere he sees here a hint of the idea of a cenotaph. Gregory Nagy stresses the final word, kleos: Andromache acknowledges that Hector's concern was always the glory he would have among the Trojans. The book closes with the women's answering lament (22.515), and the question of Hector's burial is left for Book 24.
